graders.name: 01-output-records-a-map-with-bearings-filled-and-a-
graders.evidence:
I started a plan file at `plans/per-device-session-revocation.md`. This repo is empty, so I couldn't check your auth code. What follows is a proposed way to separate the three terms, not a finding from your code.

## The three terms, separated

```
Account ──1:N──▶ Session ──1:N──▶ Tokens
 (you)           (one sign-in on       refresh token: long-lived, tied to the session
                  one client)          access tokens: short-lived, issued from the refresh token
                    │
                    └─ device info: browser/app, IP, name, last seen
                       (a label for display, not its own entity)
```

- **Session** is what you actually revoke. It's one sign-in on one client, created at login and ended by logout, revocation or expiry.
- **Device** is how the session looks to the user. It's a description stored on the session, not a separate table. You can't reliably tell physical hardware apart: Chrome and Firefox on one laptop are two sessions, and that's correct. So "per-device revocation" really means per-session revocation, shown to the user as devices.
- **Tokens** are what a session gives out. Revoking a session makes its refresh token stop working. Its access tokens keep working until they expire unless each request checks whether the session is still alive. That trade-off (how fast a sign-out takes effect vs. the cost of checking on every request) is the one hard choice in this feature. I've parked it until I know your stack.

## Proposed goal (tell me if you'd agree to it)

> A signed-in user can see every place their account is signed in, each labelled by device, and sign out any one of them so that client loses access within a known time limit, while the others stay signed in.

## Two questions before I lay out the decisions

1. **What's your auth stack?** Where does the code live, and is it server-side session cookies, stateless JWTs, or a hosted provider like Auth0, Clerk or Cognito? This largely decides the latency trade-off. If you point me at the repo, I'll read it instead of asking you more.
2. **How much effort is this worth to you?** For example, a small self-serve "sign out other devices" button, or a full sessions page with admin tools. I won't guess.

Once you answer, the next step is listing the open decisions: who can revoke (the user, admins, or both), how fast a sign-out has to take effect, what happens to the current session, how sessions get their device labels, and whether a password change signs everything out. If this breakdown of the terms holds up, I'll also add it to a `CONTEXT.md` glossary so later sessions use the same names.

graders.name: 01-output-records-a-map-with-bearings-filled-and-a-
graders.evidence:
I started a planning file at `plans/per-device-session-revocation.md`. The working directory is empty, so there's no existing auth code for me to look at. Most of the design depends on your stack, so I need two answers from you before I lay out the decisions.

## The three terms, separated

```
User ──< Device ──< Session ──< Token(s)
          label      what gets    credentials that
         (display)   revoked      prove the session
```

- **Device:** the thing you recognise, like "Chrome on MacBook" or "iPhone app." It's a label for display and grouping, not a security boundary, because a device ID reported by the client can be faked.
- **Session:** one server-side record of one sign-in. It's created when the user logs in and ends at logout, expiry, or revocation. **Revocation acts on this record.**
- **Token:** a credential the client sends to prove it has a session. A short-lived access token and a longer-lived refresh token both point back to one session. A token proves a session; it isn't the session.

With those separated, "revoke a device" means: end the session(s) shown under that device label, and make every token tied to them stop working. The real design questions follow from that. How quickly must an access token that's already been issued stop working? Does one device hold one session, or several? How do we tell a device apart from the others?

## Proposed goal

> A signed-in user can see every device that holds a live session on their account and revoke any one of them, which cuts that device off within a stated time limit and leaves every other device signed in.

Is that what you want? Change anything that's off. For example, should admins also be able to revoke devices for a user?

## Two questions

1. **What does auth look like today?** Stateless JWTs, server-side sessions with cookies, a hosted provider (Auth0, Clerk, Cognito, Supabase…), or nothing yet? This matters most. With stateless JWTs, revocation needs a denylist or very short token lifetimes. With server-side sessions, it's mostly a delete.
2. **How much effort is this worth to you?** For example, a small feature or a larger overhaul of auth.

Once you answer, I'll go through the open decisions a round at a time: how one device relates to its sessions, how fast a revoked device must be cut off, how devices are identified, and what the user sees. Each will come with a recommendation and its main weakness.

graders.name: 01-output-records-a-map-with-bearings-filled-and-a-
graders.evidence:
Nothing to resume: there's no `CONTEXT.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and no `plans/` folder. This directory is also empty, so I can't look at your auth code. The map will go in `plans/per-device-session-revocation.md` once the destination below is settled.

## The three terms, pulled apart

| Term | What it is | Lifetime | Its job in this feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Device** | What the user sees in a list, like "iPhone · Safari · Berlin". It's built from the user-agent, IP and a name. | As long as you keep the row | **What the user sees.** It's a label, not a security boundary, because you can't reliably identify hardware. |
| **Session** | A single sign-in. It starts at login and ends at logout, revocation or expiry. | Days to months | **What you revoke.** Revoking a session is the actual feature. |
| **Token** | The credential that proves a session exists. Usually a short-lived access token plus a long-lived refresh token. | Minutes (access) to weeks (refresh). Tokens get replaced over time. | **What gets rejected.** A token is only as revocable as the server check it goes through. |

The short version: **you revoke sessions and show them to users as devices, and tokens are how the revocation takes effect.** "Per-device" usually means one row per session, labelled with its device info.

Where this gets tricky is how quickly a revocation takes effect. If your access tokens are stateless JWTs that are never checked against the server, a revoked device keeps working until its access token expires. That trade-off will probably be the first thing we have to decide on the map.

## Candidate destination

> A signed-in user can see every place they're signed in and end any one of them. That client then loses access within a known, bounded time.

## Two questions before I build the map

1. **Is that destination right?** Or does "per-device" mean something more to you, like trusted devices, device limits, or remembering a device across logins? If you're not sure, say so and I'll treat it as an open question instead of forcing an answer.
2. **What's your current auth setup, and how much time do you want to spend on this?** For example: server-side cookie sessions, JWT access and refresh tokens, or a provider like Auth0, Clerk or Supabase. And is this a few days of work or a bigger rework of auth? The repo is empty, so I can't find this myself.

Once you've answered, I'll create the map and go through the open decisions with you one round at a time. The first round will likely cover what a session record contains, how quickly revocation has to take effect, and how to handle existing logins.

## The three terms, pulled apart

| Term | What it is | Lifetime | Its job in this feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Device** | What the user sees in a list, like "iPhone · Safari · Berlin". It's built from the user-agent, IP and a name. | As long as you keep the row | **What the user sees.** It's a label, not a security boundary, because you can't reliably identify hardware. |
| **Session** | A single sign-in. It starts at login and ends at logout, revocation or expiry. | Days to months | **What you revoke.** Revoking a session is the actual feature. |
| **Token** | The credential that proves a session exists. Usually a short-lived access token plus a long-lived refresh token. | Minutes (access) to weeks (refresh). Tokens get replaced over time. | **What gets rejected.** A token is only as revocable as the server check it goes through. |

The short version: **you revoke sessions and show them to users as devices, and tokens are how the revocation takes effect.** "Per-device" usually means one row per session, labelled with its device info.

Where this gets tricky is how quickly a revocation takes effect. If your access tokens are stateless JWTs that are never checked against the server, a revoked device keeps working until its access token expires. That trade-off will probably be the first thing we have to decide on the map.
